pos: n. (the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the first stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew aleph, an ox, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Aleph by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Aleph is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet and stands as the heading of the first stanza of Psalm 119, where the Authorized Version prints it in the text itself: “ALEPH. Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the LORD” (Psalm 119:1). The psalm is an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the alphabet, and all eight verses of a stanza begin in Hebrew with that letter. The name aleph is the ox — the beast of the plough and of the yoke, the strength a man harnesses and sets to work. It is a fitting first letter for a psalm about the law, for the law is a yoke laid upon the neck of a willing servant. The stanza itself opens not with a petition but with a benediction, and that order is doctrine: before the psalmist asks anything he pronounces the blessedness of the man who walks in God's way. “Blessed are they that keep his testimonies, and that seek him with the whole heart” (Psalm 119:2). Then, having seen the blessedness, he groans after it: “O that my ways were directed to keep thy statutes!” (Psalm 119:5). The stanza ends where every honest obedience ends, with a plea not to be let go: “I will keep thy statutes: O forsake me not utterly” (Psalm 119:8). That the first letter a Hebrew child learned should carry the first beatitude of the law is a kindness of the Holy Ghost.

corruption_summary: The opening beatitude of the law is read as a sentimental wish rather than as the declared verdict of God upon the obedient man.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern habit is to hear “blessed” as a feeling and to make Psalm 119:1 a mood rather than a verdict. It is a verdict. God declares which man is well off, and He declares it of the undefiled in the way who walk in His law. The blessedness is not reported by the man; it is pronounced over him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the law of God is a yoke fitted to a redeemed neck, and that the first thing to be said about obedience is not that it is hard but that it is blessed.

pos: n. (the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the second stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew beth, a house or a tent, the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Beth by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Beth is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the second stanza of Psalm 119, printed in the text by the Authorized Version: “BETH. Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word” (Psalm 119:9). The name means a house or a tent, the dwelling a man builds and keeps; it is the same word that stands at the front of scores of place-names in the land — Bethel the house of God, Bethlehem the house of bread, Bethany, Beth-horon, Beth-shemesh. The letter is the dwelling-place, and the stanza it heads is about where the word of God is lodged. The psalmist asks the plainest practical question in the psalm — how a young man is to keep himself clean — and answers it without a shred of mysticism: by taking heed to the word. Then he names the lodging: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psalm 119:11). A word kept on a shelf cleanses nothing; a word housed in the heart keeps a man from sinning. The stanza closes as it must: “I will delight myself in thy statutes: I will not forget thy word” (Psalm 119:16). The letter of the house teaches that Scripture is not a visitor to be entertained but a tenant to be settled.

corruption_summary: Scripture memory is treated as a childhood exercise outgrown rather than as the appointed means by which a man is kept from sin.
corruption_paragraphs: The word hidden in the heart has been downgraded to a Sunday-school craft. Psalm 119:11 gives it as the mechanism of holiness: the word lodged inside is what stands between a man and his sin at the hour the temptation comes, when no book is open and no teacher is near. A generation that has outsourced its memory to its devices has quietly surrendered the one weapon this verse puts in its hand.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that cleansing comes by the word taken heed to and housed within, and that the question of Psalm 119:9 still has only the one answer it is given there.

pos: n. (the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the third stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew gimel, a camel, the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Gimel by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Gimel is the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the third stanza of Psalm 119, which the Authorized Version prints in the verse: “GIMEL. Deal bountifully with thy servant, that I may live, and keep thy word” (Psalm 119:17). The name is the camel, the beast that carries a load across a wilderness and needs no water on the way. It is the right letter for this stanza, for the stanza is the cry of a traveller. The psalmist calls himself what Abraham called himself and what Peter calls the whole church: “I am a stranger in the earth: hide not thy commandments from me” (Psalm 119:19). A pilgrim needs two things, provision and a map, and he asks for both — that God would deal bountifully with him, and that God would open his eyes: “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Psalm 119:18). That petition is the whole Reformed doctrine of illumination in nine words. The law does not lack wonders; the reader lacks eyes, and only God opens them. The stanza ends with the traveller's company: “Thy testimonies also are my delight and my counsellors” (Psalm 119:24). Princes sat and spoke against him; the testimonies sat and counselled him. The camel-letter marks the stanza of the man who is carrying the word through a country that is not his home.

corruption_summary: The prayer for opened eyes is replaced by confidence in technique, as though the wonders of the law were a matter of better method rather than of granted sight.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 119:18 is a prayer, and the modern reader has turned it into a procedure. Study aids multiply, and they are good, but no apparatus opens a blind eye. The Reformed doctrine of illumination holds that the Spirit who gave the word must also give the sight to see it; the natural man receives it not, and no amount of apparatus makes him receive it.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Christian reads Scripture as a stranger in the earth who must ask for eyes before he asks for insight.

pos: n. (the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the fourth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew daleth, a door, the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Daleth by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Daleth is the fourth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the fourth stanza of Psalm 119, printed in the text by the Authorized Version: “DALETH. My soul cleaveth unto the dust: quicken thou me according to thy word” (Psalm 119:25). The name is the door — the hung leaf that swings on its hinge, the thing that is either shut against a man or opened to him. It heads the lowest stanza in the psalm. The soul here is in the dust, melting for heaviness, and it asks twice for the same thing in the same terms: “My soul melteth for heaviness: strengthen thou me according unto thy word” (Psalm 119:28). Twice the measure of the mercy sought is the word of God, for a sufferer who asks according to his feelings asks blindly, while a sufferer who asks according to the word asks for what God has bound Himself to give. The stanza then turns, and the turn is the door opening: “I have chosen the way of truth: thy judgments have I laid before me” (Psalm 119:30), and at the last the man who lay in the dust is running — “I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart” (Psalm 119:32). Quickening comes first and running follows; the heart is enlarged by God before the feet move. The letter of the door marks the stanza in which God opens one. Daleth is the letter and is not the English dale, a valley, with which its spelling has nothing to do.

corruption_summary: Heaviness of soul is handled as a disorder to be managed rather than as an affliction to be carried to God and answered from His word.
corruption_paragraphs: A soul cleaving to the dust is now first of all a case to be treated, and the vocabulary of therapy has very nearly replaced the vocabulary of prayer. The psalmist does not deny his heaviness or explain it away; he names it plainly and then asks to be quickened, and he asks according to the word rather than according to his own sense of what would help. That is the shape of biblical lament, and it ends in running.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the afflicted believer prays according to the word, and that God enlarges the heart before He requires the race.

pos: n. (the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the seventh stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew zayin, a weapon or a sword, the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Zain by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Zain is the seventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the seventh stanza of Psalm 119, printed in the text by the Authorized Version: “ZAIN. Remember the word unto thy servant, upon which thou hast caused me to hope” (Psalm 119:49). The name is a weapon, the sword or the dagger; the old grammarians took the letter's shape for a blade. It heads a stanza fought under fire. The proud have the psalmist in derision, horror takes hold of him because of the wicked, and his one weapon is a remembered word: “This is my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickened me” (Psalm 119:50). Note the order of the remembering. He asks God to remember the word to him, and then he does the remembering himself: “I remembered thy judgments of old, O LORD; and have comforted myself” (Psalm 119:52). A Christian under derision is not helpless; he has a magazine of old judgments to draw on, and drawing on them is how he comforts himself. The stanza gives the sweetest line in the psalm for a pilgrim: “Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psalm 119:54). The sword-letter marks the stanza in which the word is both the weapon and the song.

corruption_summary: Comfort is sought in distraction or in sentiment rather than in the remembered judgments of God, which is where this stanza puts it.
corruption_paragraphs: The believer under derision is counselled on every side to seek relief, and almost never to seek it where Psalm 119:52 seeks it — in the judgments of God from of old. The psalmist comforts himself by an act of memory about God's dealings, not by an act of escape from his circumstances. That is a discipline, and it can be learned.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the statutes of God are songs for the house of our pilgrimage, and that a word remembered is a weapon drawn.

pos: n. (the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the eighth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew cheth, a fence or an enclosure, the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Cheth by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Cheth is the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the eighth stanza of Psalm 119, which the Authorized Version prints in the verse: “CHETH. Thou art my portion, O LORD: I have said that I would keep thy words” (Psalm 119:57). The name is a fence or an enclosure, a wall thrown round a thing to mark it off and to keep it. It is the fitting letter for a stanza of portion and of boundary, and it should not be confused with Heth the son of Canaan, the father of the Hittites, who shares the English spelling in some hands but is another thing altogether. The psalmist takes God Himself as his inheritance, which is the Levite's portion extended to every believer, and from that portion flows a resolve about time: “I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments” (Psalm 119:60). Obedience in this stanza is prompt, and it is also nocturnal: “At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee because of thy righteous judgments” (Psalm 119:62). The bands of the wicked robbed him and he did not forget the law; the enclosure held. And the fence does not shut out the world's company but gathers the right company in: “I am a companion of all them that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts” (Psalm 119:63).

corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 119:63 fixes the ground of fellowship: a companion of all them that fear God and keep His precepts. Not all them who share an interest, a stage of life, or a temperament. The modern congregation sorts itself by affinity and then wonders why its fellowship is thin; the psalmist sorts by the fear of the LORD and finds the whole company of the faithful opened to him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God Himself is the believer's portion, and that a man who has that portion makes haste to obey and does not delay.

pos: n. (the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the eleventh stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew kaph, the palm of the hand, the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Caph by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Caph is the eleventh letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the eleventh stanza of Psalm 119, printed in the text by the Authorized Version: “CAPH. My soul fainteth for thy salvation: but I hope in thy word” (Psalm 119:81). The name is the palm of the hand, the open hollow hand — the hand held out empty to receive, or bent to hold. It heads the stanza of longest waiting. Twice the psalmist is at the end of his strength: his soul faints, and then “Mine eyes fail for thy word, saying, When wilt thou comfort me?” (Psalm 119:82). He gives himself the strangest image in the psalm for what the waiting has done to him: “For I am become like a bottle in the smoke; yet do I not forget thy statutes” (Psalm 119:83) — a skin bottle hung in the rafters above the fire, blackened, shrivelled, dried hard. That is a man who has been waiting on God a long while and has not let go. The stanza is honest about the cause: the proud have digged pits, they persecute him wrongfully. And it ends with the open palm held out for the only thing that will serve: “Quicken me after thy lovingkindness; so shall I keep the testimony of thy mouth” (Psalm 119:88). The letter of the empty hand marks the stanza of the believer who has nothing left but the word he hopes in.

corruption_summary: Long waiting on God is read as evidence that something has gone wrong, rather than as the ordinary experience of faith which this stanza describes without apology.
corruption_paragraphs: A faith that faints and eyes that fail are treated as symptoms of a defect, and the believer who is still waiting is urged to find the blockage. Psalm 119:81-88 knows no such counsel. The man is dried like a bottle in the smoke and he has not forgotten the statutes; the waiting is the trial, not the proof of failure, and the bottle in the smoke is in the inspired text precisely so that the long waiter should know he is not an anomaly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hope in the word outlasts the strength of the soul that holds it, and that quickening is asked after God's lovingkindness and not after our deserving.

pos: n. (the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the sixteenth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew ayin, an eye, the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Ain by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Ain is the sixteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the sixteenth stanza of Psalm 119, which the Authorized Version prints in the verse: “AIN. I have done judgment and justice: leave me not to mine oppressors” (Psalm 119:121). The name is the eye, and by a natural extension a spring of water, the eye of the land from which it weeps. The letter should not be confused with the town of Ain in the south country, which the dictionary treats separately. It is the right letter for this stanza, for the stanza is full of looking: “Mine eyes fail for thy salvation, and for the word of thy righteousness” (Psalm 119:123). The psalmist has done judgment and justice and is still in the hands of oppressors, and so he asks God to stand as his bondsman: “Be surety for thy servant for good: let not the proud oppress me” (Psalm 119:122). Then comes the verse that every reformer has prayed in a dark hour — “It is time for thee, LORD, to work: for they have made void thy law” (Psalm 119:126). When men void God's law, the remedy sought is not the arm of the godly but the working of God. The stanza ends in a settled valuation: “Therefore I love thy commandments above gold; yea, above fine gold” (Psalm 119:127), and in a settled hatred of every false way.

corruption_summary: When the law of God is voided in a nation, the first recourse is sought in political leverage rather than in the working of God which this stanza begs for.
corruption_paragraphs: “It is time for thee, LORD, to work” is the prayer of a man who has watched the law of God set aside and who knows where the remedy lies. The instinct of our age is to reach first for leverage, and the believer who reaches first for God is thought to have done nothing. The psalmist has in fact done judgment and justice himself (Psalm 119:121); he is not idle. But he does not mistake his own hand for the arm that must work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is the surety of His oppressed servant, and that the commandments are to be loved above fine gold by a man who is still waiting for deliverance.

pos: n. (the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the heading of the seventeenth stanza of Psalm 119)
etymology: Hebrew pe, a mouth, the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Pe by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Pe is the seventeenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the seventeenth stanza of Psalm 119, printed in the text by the Authorized Version: “PE. Thy testimonies are wonderful: therefore doth my soul keep them” (Psalm 119:129). The name is the mouth, the opening through which speech comes out and food goes in. It is exactly the letter this stanza wants, for the stanza is about mouths — God's and the psalmist's. First God's: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psalm 119:130). That verse is the dictionary's doctrine of the perspicuity of Scripture in a single line. The word of God does not require a priesthood of experts to unlock it; its mere entrance gives light, and the one it enlightens is named the simple. Then the psalmist's own mouth: “I opened my mouth, and panted: for I longed for thy commandments” (Psalm 119:131) — the open-mouthed gasping of a man in a hard thirst. He asks that his steps be ordered in the word and that no iniquity have dominion over him, and the stanza closes in tears for other men's disobedience: “Rivers of waters run down mine eyes, because they keep not thy law” (Psalm 119:136). A mouth that has tasted the word weeps over the mouths that will not.

corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 119:130 says the entrance of God's words gives understanding to the simple. The practical denial of that verse is everywhere: the text is said to be too distant, too conditioned by its culture, too contested for an ordinary believer to read for himself and know what it says. The Reformers answered this with the doctrine of perspicuity — what is necessary for salvation is plain in Scripture to the diligent reader with the Spirit's help — and the answer has not needed amending.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a believer who has tasted the word longs for it with an open mouth and weeps over the lawlessness of other men rather than growing used to it.

etymology: Hebrew tsadhe, a fish-hook, the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; rendered Tzaddi by the Authorized Version in the headings of Psalm 119.
biblical_def: Tzaddi is the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet and heads the eighteenth stanza of Psalm 119, which the Authorized Version prints in the verse: “TZADDI. Righteous art thou, O LORD, and upright are thy judgments” (Psalm 119:137). The old grammarians named the letter a fish-hook from its shape, and it shares its consonants with tsedeq, righteousness — which is the word this stanza is built on. Four times in eight verses the psalmist comes back to it: the LORD is righteous, His testimonies are righteous, His righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, the righteousness of His testimonies is everlasting. And he says the thing plainly that the whole psalm has been circling: “Thy righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and thy law is the truth” (Psalm 119:142). The law is not one account of the truth; it is the truth. From that confession two things follow in the stanza. The first is zeal: “My zeal hath consumed me, because mine enemies have forgotten thy words” (Psalm 119:139). The second is love for the word's purity: “Thy word is very pure: therefore thy servant loveth it” (Psalm 119:140). And the man who says all this calls himself small and despised, and does not forget the precepts. The hook-letter marks the stanza where God's righteousness takes hold and does not let a man go.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Tzaddi is the name of a Hebrew letter and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.
webster_full: Tzaddi is the name of the eighteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

corruption_summary: The law of God is demoted to one witness among many, when Psalm 119:142 says flatly that it is the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: “Thy law is the truth” leaves no room for the treatment of Scripture as a perspective to be set beside others and weighed. The modern habit of ranking the law of God among competing accounts of the good is not a refinement of this verse; it is a contradiction of it. Where the law is the truth, a departure from it is not a different reading but a lie.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that zeal for God's words is proper to a believer who sees them forgotten, and that the smallness and contempt of the faithful man alters nothing about the everlasting righteousness he stands on.
